summary: This bill amends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to prohibit employers from taking adverse actions against employees for expressing that sex is binary or biological (including via pronouns) or for requesting single-sex bathrooms and changing areas.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act solely to add employment protections for certain speech and conduct related to biological sex. It contains no appropriations, authorizations, or changes to federal spending levels.
No provisions alter tax rates, deductions, credits, or revenue collection.
The bill does not address insurance coverage, medical services, or healthcare delivery systems.
No references to firearms, Second Amendment issues, or related regulations.
No provisions concerning visas, border policy, or immigration status.
No language addressing reproductive rights or abortion access.
No impact on defense budgets, military policy, or national security spending.
No environmental, regulatory, or climate-related provisions.
No changes to welfare programs, entitlements, or social services eligibility.
The bill is referred to the Education and Workforce Committee but contains no education funding, curriculum, or school policy provisions.
No provisions related to controlled substances or drug enforcement.
No sentencing, policing, or criminal procedure changes.
No trade agreements, tariffs, or import/export rules.
No fiscal policy, deficit, or debt provisions.

The bill explicitly protects employees who assert the binary/biological nature of sex, including pronoun usage and single-sex facility requests. This directly counters the expansion of Title VII protections for gender identity (post-Bostock) by shielding speech and conduct that rejects transgender or non-binary identities. It therefore limits legal protections for LGBTQ+ individuals in the workplace.
No foreign policy or aid provisions.
No election administration, voting access, or campaign finance content.
No data privacy, technology regulation, or surveillance provisions.
No collective bargaining, union rights, or labor relations changes.

While the protected expression could overlap with religious beliefs about sex, the bill is framed exclusively around biological assertions rather than religious exemptions or civil-rights balancing. No explicit religious-liberty language appears.
